newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Euro-speak haunts EU treaty talks.
newsitem.headline: Euro-speak haunts EU treaty talks.

text.p: Citizens beware! A new European Union treaty is being written, embellished with the usual burst of Euro-babble.
Leaders of the 15-nation EU meet in the Dutch coastal resort of Noordwijk on Friday to discuss the treaty ahead of a planned agreement at another summit in Amsterdam in June.
Despite pledging to make the new treaty meaningful to the average citizen, negotiators have easily slipped into Euro-speak, creating convoluted terms for the already complex issues under discussion.

Start with the title of the treaty talks themselves, formally known as the INTER-GOVERNMENTAL CONFERENCE. For English speakers the term brought immediate confusion, suggesting a one- or two-day meeting.
In fact the conference, in the French sense of conferring, began in March 1996 and has been running ever since.
One key issue has been what to do to improve the THIRD PILLAR.

This term was inherited from the Maastricht Treaty where a system was created to allow EU countries to act together on foreign policy (SECOND PILLAR) and in such matters as crime-fighting and asylum (THIRD PILLAR).
In these areas, countries were to take decisions among themselves rather than through the EU's institutions, such as the European Commission and European Parliament (FIRST or COMMUNITY PILLAR).

If that wasn't complicated enough, there has been talk in the current negotiations of creating a PASSERELLE from the third pillar to the first, or of COMMUNITARISING it. Translation: getting the Commission and Parliament involved -- theoretically to make it more efficient.

The EU also wants to make its CFSP, or COMMON FOREIGN AND SECURITY POLICY, more efficient and to have a stronger voice on the world stage. CFSP has historically meant issuing statements expressing concern or delight at various foreign adventures.
One suggestion for reversing this has been to appoint a MONSIEUR PESC -- French for Mr CFSP -- a high-level appointee who would be called upon to coordinate EU foreign policy.

Some officials, wary of male-dominated Brussels, go out of their way to say he could be a Madame or a Mrs. He or she could also play a role in a revamped TROIKA -- the three foreign ministers from past, present and future six-month EU presidencies.
Things get even more opaque for the beleaguered EU citizen when it comes to deciding how to pass laws.

Although many say the process should involve TRANSPARENCY -- meaning the public should be able to follow it -- it currently involves such concepts as "A" POINTS, QUALIFIED MAJORITY VOTING, CO-DECISION, and now DOUBLE MAJORITY VOTING.
Overall, SUBSIDIARITY will rule, meaning that laws should be passed at the lowest relevant level of government.
The science of tracking all this decision making, by the way, is called COMITOLOGY.
